findings.title: Operator "suspend family" is bypassed by every non-session auth path (kiosk token, MCP token, a2a HMAC)
findings.description:
The 2026-07-26 super-admin work made `families.is_active` "genuinely enforced" — but only in `get_current_user` (dependencies.py:73-78) and the Google login path (google_oauth_service.py:272-276). Four other authenticated entry points that do NOT go through `get_current_user` were missed: they check `Family.deleted_at` but never `Family.is_active`.

- `KioskService.get_snapshot` (kiosk_service.py:337-338) and `KioskService.resolve_pin_view` (kiosk_service.py:216-217) — a provisioned wall-display token keeps serving the full family snapshot (member names, roles, points, today's chores, shopping lists, calendar) after suspension.
- `TokenService.resolve` (jarvis_mcp_token_service.py:61-69) — the `/mcp` join filters `Family.deleted_at.is_(None)` only, so a family-scoped MCP bearer token keeps full CRUD (including money-moving `points_adjust_create`, `budget_transaction_delete`) on a suspended family.
- `_family_and_secret` (api/routes/budget/bank_sync.py:41-49) — checks `cfg.enabled` only, so the bank-email-matcher agent keeps creating and reconciling budget transactions on a suspended (and even a soft-deleted) family.

The design spec explicitly promises suspension "Locks out all members immediately" (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-26-super-admin-dashboard-design.md:293). `tests/test_family_suspension.py` covers login / existing token / refresh / Google sign-in — none of the four token paths above.
findings.evidence:
kiosk_service.py:337-338 — `family = await db.get(Family, family_id)` / `if family is not None and family.deleted_at is not None: raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Account closed")` — no `is_active` check, unlike dependencies.py:73 `if family_active is False: raise HTTPException(401, "Family suspended")`.

jarvis_mcp_token_service.py:64-68 — `.where(JarvisMcpToken.token_hash == token_hash, JarvisMcpToken.revoked_at.is_(None), Family.deleted_at.is_(None),)`

bank_sync.py:47-48 — `if cfg is None or not cfg.enabled: raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, "family not registered")`
findings.recommendation: Add a single shared helper (e.g. `assert_family_usable(family)` raising 401 on `deleted_at is not None` OR `is_active is False`) and call it from all four sites. For `TokenService.resolve` and `_family_and_secret` add `Family.is_active.is_(True)` to the query; for bank_sync also add the missing `Family.deleted_at.is_(None)` guard. Extend `tests/test_family_suspension.py` with one case per path (kiosk snapshot, kiosk pin-view, /mcp bearer, a2a signed POST) so the next auth surface can't silently reopen the hole.

findings.title: /api/oauth/google is unauthenticated, unrate-limited, and blocks the event loop on an outbound HTTPS call
findings.description:
`POST /api/oauth/google` is a public route (listed in frontend/src/middleware.ts:241 `publicRoutes`) that creates users and whole families. Unlike every sibling auth endpoint it carries no `@limiter.limit`: auth.py decorates register-family (78), login (94), check-methods (170), verify-email (301), resend-verification (318), forgot-password (338), reset-password (356). oauth.py decorates nothing.

Two compounding problems:

1. **Blocking IO on the event loop.** The first thing the handler does is `await GoogleOAuthService.verify_google_token(...)`, which calls the *synchronous* `id_token.verify_oauth2_token(token, requests.Request(), audience=None)` (google_oauth_service.py:123). I read the installed library: `verify_token` calls `_fetch_certs(request, certs_url)` on every invocation (site-packages/google/oauth2/id_token.py:130) with no cache — a blocking HTTPS GET to googleapis.com per request, on the asyncio thread. The PayPal webhook route does the equivalent correctly (`await asyncio.to_thread(PayPalService.verify_webhook_signature, ...)`, subscriptions_webhook.py:106). With `--workers 2` (docker-compose.onprem.yml:95) a trivial unauthenticated request flood stalls both event loops of a box shared with school-admin/medical/platform.

2. **Unbounded join-code oracle.** The same endpoint accepts `join_code`; an invalid code returns 400 "Invalid join code" while a valid one returns 403 `approval_pending` (google_oauth_service.py:305 vs 463). Join codes are 6 chars from a 31-symbol alphabet (models/family.py:11-15, ~8.9e8 space). The password join path is throttled at AUTH_LIMIT; this one is not, and one Google ID token can be replayed for the full hour of its validity.

The frontend proxy also drops the real client IP: src/pages/api/oauth/google.ts:24-27 sends only `Content-Type`, unlike the auth proxies which call `clientIpHeaders(request)` (src/lib/client-ip.ts) precisely so the backend limiter keys on the real user — so even adding a limiter here would collapse all browser traffic into one bucket until that is fixed too.
findings.evidence:
oauth.py:50-54 — `@router.post("/google", response_model=TokenResponse, status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)` / `async def google_oauth_login(request: GoogleTokenRequest = Body(...), db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),):` — no `@limiter.limit`.

google_oauth_service.py:123-127 — `idinfo = id_token.verify_oauth2_token(token, requests.Request(), audience=None,)` (sync call inside `async def`).

site-packages/google/oauth2/id_token.py:130 — `certs = _fetch_certs(request, certs_url)` — refetched on every call.
findings.recommendation: Add `@limiter.limit(AUTH_LIMIT)` to both `google_oauth_login` and `verify_google_token` (oauth.py:50, 128) and give the routes the `request: Request` param slowapi needs. Wrap the verification in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (or use an async transport) so cert fetching never blocks the loop, and cache Google's certs for their `Cache-Control` lifetime. Add `...clientIpHeaders(request)` to the fetch headers in frontend/src/pages/api/oauth/google.ts so the limiter keys per user rather than per frontend container.

findings.title: Google sign-in links an existing password account by email without requiring email_verified
findings.description:
`authenticate_or_create_user` falls back to an email lookup when no `oauth_id` match exists, and unconditionally attaches the presenting Google identity to that pre-existing account, then issues a full access+refresh pair for it. The `email_verified` claim from the ID token is read only to *upgrade* our own `email_verified` flag — it is never used as a precondition for the link itself.

This is the classic "Sign in with Google" pre-hijacking / unverified-email account-takeover pattern: any Google identity whose `email` claim equals a victim's account email (Cloud Identity / Workspace identities can carry `email_verified: false`) authenticates as that victim, inheriting their role — including PARENT — and their `family_id`. That is a direct cross-tenant escalation: the attacker lands inside another family with full session tokens.

Note the surrounding code is otherwise careful about exactly this class of problem — the role-selection block below (lines 375-394) has a long comment explaining why nothing in the unauthenticated payload may be trusted — which makes the missing guard here look like an oversight rather than a decision.
findings.evidence: google_oauth_service.py:243-255 — `if not user:` / `user = (await db.execute(select(User).where(User.email == email))).scalar_one_or_none()` / `# If found by email, link the Google account` / `if user:` / `user.oauth_provider = "google"` / `user.oauth_id = google_id` / `if google_user_info.get('email_verified'): user.email_verified = True` / `await db.commit()` — then line 284 mints `create_access_token(...)` for that account.
findings.recommendation: Refuse the link when `google_user_info['email_verified']` is not true — raise `UnauthorizedException` and force the user through the password login + explicit "connect Google" flow from an authenticated session. Consider also refusing the silent link entirely for accounts that already have a `password_hash` (require re-authentication before binding a new identity provider). Add a regression test alongside `tests/test_family_suspension.py::test_suspended_family_cannot_google_sign_in`.

findings.title: Budget backup import trusts arbitrary foreign keys from a user-supplied ZIP, crossing the tenant boundary
findings.description:
`ExportService.import_budget` rebuilds every row straight from the uploaded JSON via `model_cls(**item_dict)`, overriding only `family_id`. Every *other* column — including the primary key `id` and the foreign keys `account_id`, `category_id`, `payee_id`, `group_id`, `transfer_account_id` — is taken verbatim from the untrusted file. The FK constraints point at the global tables, so a row in family A referencing family B's `budget_categories.id` inserts cleanly.

This is the only path in the budget domain that skips ownership validation: the normal write path validates every FK against the caller's family (`transaction_service.py:90` `await AccountService.get_by_id(db, data.account_id, family_id)`, `:95` `CategoryService.get_by_id(..., family_id)`, `:102` `PayeeService.get_by_id(..., family_id)`).

The consequence is observable because the reporting join is scoped only on the transaction side: `ReportService` joins `BudgetTransaction -> BudgetCategory -> BudgetCategoryGroup` with `BudgetTransaction.family_id == family_id` as the sole tenant predicate, so an injected row renders another family's category and group *names* into family A's spending report. Balance math happens to be safe (`account_service.py:446` filters `BudgetTransaction.family_id`), which is why this has gone unnoticed.

Exploitability is bounded by having to know a target UUID, so I am rating this medium rather than high — but the row-level tenant boundary is genuinely broken here, and the import endpoint is available to any parent on any plan (`export.py:41-45` gates on `require_parent_role` only).
findings.evidence:
export_service.py:189-197 — `for item_dict in items:` / `# Override family_id to current family` / `item_dict["family_id"] = family_id` / `_convert_uuids(item_dict, model_cls)` / `_convert_dates(item_dict, model_cls)` / `obj = model_cls(**item_dict)` / `db.add(obj)`

report_service.py:76-85 — `.select_from(BudgetTransaction)` / `.join(BudgetCategory, BudgetTransaction.category_id == BudgetCategory.id)` / `.join(BudgetCategoryGroup, BudgetCategory.group_id == BudgetCategoryGroup.id)` / `.where(and_(BudgetTransaction.family_id == family_id, ...))` — no family predicate on the joined category/group.
findings.recommendation: In `import_budget`, drop client-supplied `id` values (let the DB mint new ones) and remap intra-archive FK references through an old-id -> new-id dict built as each entity type is imported; reject the whole archive if a reference does not resolve within the archive. Whitelist the accepted keys per model instead of splatting the dict. Independently, add `BudgetCategory.family_id == family_id` (and the group equivalent) to the report joins as defence in depth.

findings.title: Budget backup import decompresses the uploaded ZIP with no uncompressed-size cap (zip bomb)
findings.description:
`import_budget` opens the uploaded archive and calls `zf.read("budget_data.json")` — reading the entire decompressed member into memory in one shot — then `json.loads` on the result. The only limit anywhere in the path is on the *compressed* upload: `read_upload_capped(file, MAX_BACKUP_BYTES)` with `MAX_BACKUP_BYTES = 25 * MB` (core/upload_validation.py:16). DEFLATE reaches ~1000:1 on repetitive input, so a 25 MB upload can expand to tens of GB before any of our code inspects it.

The endpoint requires only `require_parent_role` (api/routes/budget/export.py:41-45) — no premium gate — so any free-tier signup can OOM-kill a uvicorn worker. Production runs `--workers 2` on 10.1.0.91, a box shared with school-admin, medical, platform and vault, so the blast radius is not limited to this app.

The repo already has the right pattern for capped reads (`read_upload_capped`); it just is not applied on the decompression side.
findings.evidence:
export_service.py:151-154 — `buf = io.BytesIO(zip_bytes)` / `with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "r") as zf:` / `data_str = zf.read("budget_data.json").decode("utf-8")` / `budget_data = json.loads(data_str)`

core/upload_validation.py:16 — `MAX_BACKUP_BYTES = 25 * MB        # full budget export ZIP (JSON-in-ZIP, small)` — caps the compressed bytes only.
findings.recommendation: Before reading, inspect `zf.getinfo("budget_data.json").file_size` and reject over a sane ceiling (the comment says these archives are small — a few MB is generous); also reject archives whose total `sum(i.file_size for i in zf.infolist())` or compression ratio is implausible. Then stream the member with `zf.open(...)` reading in bounded chunks rather than `zf.read()`, so a lying header cannot bypass the check.

findings.title: a2a bank-sync HMAC signatures carry no timestamp or nonce, so signed writes are replayable forever
findings.description:
The three machine-to-machine endpoints for the bank-email-matcher agent authenticate with a per-family HMAC over either `"candidates:<days>"` or the raw request body. The comparison itself is correct (`hmac.compare_digest`), but the signed message contains no timestamp, nonce, or expiry — a captured request is valid indefinitely, and there is no binding between the signature and the endpoint being called.

Impact is limited because the two write endpoints are idempotent (`/reconcile` sets `cleared = True`; `/transactions` dedupes on `imported_id`), and TLS terminates at the Cloudflare edge — hence the low rating. It matters mainly because the secret is long-lived (`FamilyA2AWebhook.secret`, no rotation in `A2AWebhookService`) and the `candidates` message is a fixed string per `days` value, so a single observed signature grants permanent read access to a family's recent transaction ledger (dates, amounts, payee names, card last-4).
findings.evidence:
bank_sync.py:52-55 — `def _verify(secret: str, message: bytes, signature: str) -> None:` / `expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode("utf-8"), message, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()` / `if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature or ""): raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, "bad signature")`

Callers pass only the payload: line 67 `_verify(secret, f"candidates:{days}".encode("utf-8"), x_a2a_signature)`, lines 112 and 159 `_verify(secret, raw, x_a2a_signature)`.
findings.recommendation: Add an `X-A2A-Timestamp` header, include it (plus the HTTP method and path) in the signed message, and reject skew beyond ~5 minutes. Track recently-seen `(family_id, signature)` pairs in Redis for the skew window to make replay impossible rather than merely time-boxed. Update the matcher agent and `docs` in the same change.

findings.title: Operator actions leave no audit row when the underlying service raises an unexpected exception type
findings.description:
The module docstring promises that "a failed action still leaves a record of the failure rather than nothing at all", and most actions honour it with a bare `except Exception as exc` routed through `_record_failure`. Three of the ten actions narrow the catch and so silently fall outside that guarantee:

- `release_paycheck` catches `except HTTPException` only (line 570) — `BankService.release_chore_paycheck` can surface `FamilyAppException` subclasses and plain DB errors.
- `undo_chore_approval` catches `(HTTPException, FamilyAppException)` (line 651).
- `restore_recycled` catches `(HTTPException, FamilyAppException)` (line 728).

In all three the audit row is *staged before* the mutation, so an escaping `IntegrityError`/`ValueError` means the request-scoped session is rolled back by `get_db` and neither the mutation nor any audit row survives — the operator sees a 500 and the append-only trail shows nothing was ever attempted. That is the exact scenario `_record_failure` was written for.

Rated low because no incorrect data results and the failure is still on the server log — this is a completeness gap in a control the spec sells as complete, not a live vulnerability.
findings.evidence:
admin_action_service.py:570 — `except HTTPException as exc:` (release_paycheck); :651 — `except (HTTPException, FamilyAppException) as exc:` (undo_chore_approval); :728 — `except (HTTPException, FamilyAppException) as exc:` (restore_recycled).

Contrast admin_action_service.py:325 (set_user_active) — `except Exception as exc:` followed by `await _record_failure(...)`.
findings.recommendation: Widen all three to `except Exception as exc:`, keeping the existing re-raise behaviour (`raise` for the domain-exception cases so the global handlers still map the status code, and a 500 wrapper for anything else — the pattern `set_user_active` already uses). Add one test that forces a non-HTTPException failure inside a bounded action and asserts an `error` row lands in `operator_audit_log`.

findings.title: Month budget view double-counts categorized income in totals.income
findings.description: GET /api/budget/month/{year}/{month} seeds totals.income from an account-level sum of ALL positive transactions in on-budget accounts (which already includes transactions categorized to income categories), then the category loop ADDS income-group activity on top. Any deposit categorized to an income category is counted twice. The comment above the query explicitly says 'Income-category activity is a subset of this; we use the raw account-level figure' — the intent was to replace the categorized figure, but the legacy '+=' in the loop was never removed. The frontend budget dashboard consumes this directly (frontend/src/pages/budget/index.astro:65 'const totalIncome = budget?.totals?.income ?? ...'), so the summary card shows inflated income for any family that categorizes income. No test asserts totals.income, so nothing catches it. Bonus on the same line: 'income_result.scalar() or 0' skips the mandatory int() cast on a SUM over BigInteger (asyncpg returns Decimal), violating the repo's canonical aggregate-cast rule (accounts.py pattern).
findings.evidence: month.py:102 'result["totals"]["income"] = income_result.scalar() or 0' followed by month.py:149-151 '# Track income for totals reporting / if group.is_income: result["totals"]["income"] += group_data["total_activity"]'. Both are live in the same handler; git -L history shows the account-level query was added later (commit 76051878/b3c03b49) without removing the loop's +=.
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'result["totals"]["income"] += group_data["total_activity"]' branch (keep the raw account-level figure per the comment's stated intent), wrap the scalar in int(), and add a test that seeds one categorized income transaction and asserts totals.income equals it exactly once.

findings.title: Pooled DB sessions held idle-in-transaction across 60s LLM calls (receipt scan + Jarvis chat)
findings.description: Two premium LLM endpoints hold a pooled DB connection in an open transaction for the full duration of external LLM calls (LLM_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60.0, receipt_scanner_service.py:53). (1) scan_receipt_endpoint (routes/budget/transactions.py:673) passes its Depends(get_db) request session into scan_and_create_transaction, which runs a SELECT for few-shot history (line 532) — opening a transaction — and then awaits the vision call scan_receipt (line 540, up to 60s in a worker thread). The session sits 'idle in transaction' on a checked-out pool connection the whole time. (2) /api/jarvis/chat (routes/jarvis.py:69-77) passes the request session into JarvisService.chat, which runs cap-count/history/context SELECTs and then loops up to MAX_TOOL_HOPS=4 + 1 LLM completions (jarvis_service.py:634, 60s timeout each) plus tool executions on the same held session — worst case several minutes per request. Pool is pool_size=10/max_overflow=20 per worker (core/database.py:11-12) with --workers 2 in prod (docker-compose.onprem.yml:95). This is the exact failure class that caused the documented SSE idle-in-transaction 502 incident (the chat/DM/Jarvis SSE generators were fixed for it — family_chat_service.py:383-386 even documents 'the pooled connection must NOT be held across the wait window... pool exhausts → app-wide 502s' — but the non-stream request paths were not). ~15 concurrent slow scans/chats on one worker exhausts its pool and 502s the whole app.
findings.evidence: receipt_scanner_service.py:532 '_pairs = await CategorizationRuleService.recent_payee_category_pairs(db, family_id,)' then :540 'receipt = await scan_receipt(...)' (60s vision call) on the same request session; jarvis_service.py:590-596 history/context SELECTs then :634 'completion = await run_in_threadpool(...)' inside 'for hop in range(MAX_TOOL_HOPS + 1)' (MAX_TOOL_HOPS = 4, jarvis_service.py:102); core/database.py:11-12 'pool_size=10, max_overflow=20'.
findings.recommendation: Commit/close (or expunge + db.commit()) before the LLM segment and re-acquire afterwards — mirror the pattern the SSE generators already use: gather DB context in a short transaction, release the connection, run the LLM call, then open a fresh transaction to persist. For Jarvis, release the session between hops (tool calls can open their own short sessions).

findings.title: Entire PayPal billing state machine lives in route handlers (worst business-logic-in-routes offender)
findings.description: With register_family extracted and kiosk given a service, subscriptions.py is now the largest layering violation — and it is the money path. create_checkout (151-301) inline: billing-cycle validation, multi-currency plan resolution with a preference heuristic (min() over a 3-part key, lines 193-203), PayPal call, and the CRITICAL staged-pending vs in-place-refresh row state machine (ENTITLED_STATUSES / _STILL_BILLABLE_STATUSES logic, 247-296) that the comments themselves flag as double-billing protection. activate_subscription (304-451) inline: row lookup by live-or-pending PayPal id, idempotent re-entry, promote/cancel-superseded orchestration with the DOUBLE-BILLING RISK recovery path. cancel_subscription (454-509) similar. None of this is unit-testable without HTTP plumbing, and the highest-stakes invariants in the app (never double-bill, never orphan a live PayPal agreement) are encoded in a route file. Aggravating: line 224-228 'except Exception as e: raise HTTPException(500, detail=f"PayPal error: {str(e)}")' — a broad catch that (a) flattens PayPalService's typed NotFoundException/ValidationException into 500s and (b) echoes raw internal exception text (including up to 300 chars of the PayPal API response body from _PayPalV2HTTP.post) to the client.
findings.evidence: subscriptions.py:200-203 'plan = min(candidates, key=lambda p: (_paypal_id(p) is None, p.currency != "MXN", p.currency or ""))' and :266-296 the staged-pending/in-place/create row mutation block ending 'await db.commit()' — all inside the route function; :224-228 'except Exception as e: raise HTTPException(status_code=...500..., detail=f"PayPal error: {str(e)}")'.
findings.recommendation: Extract a SubscriptionCheckoutService (plan resolution, staged-pending state machine, activation/promotion, cancellation) in app/services/, leaving routes as thin HTTP adapters — the subscription_state.py helpers already exist as the natural home. Replace the broad except with catches of the specific PayPal domain exceptions and a generic operator-facing log + sanitized client message.

findings.title: Budget-vs-actual report subqueries omit the mandatory family_id filter
findings.description: The budget-vs-actual endpoint's two correlated scalar subqueries aggregate BudgetAllocation and BudgetTransaction rows filtered only by category_id + month/date — no family_id predicate — relying entirely on the outer query's 'BudgetCategory.family_id == family_id' plus the write-path guarantee that transactions/allocations only ever reference own-family categories (TransactionService validates via CategoryService.get_by_id). That guarantee currently holds, so this is defense-in-depth rather than an active leak, but it violates the codebase's hard rule that every family-scoped query filters by family_id, and it is the only aggregate in the budget module written this way (month.py, allocation_service.py, account_service.py all carry the family_id predicate in equivalent subqueries). A single future bulk-write path (import, a2a webhook, MCP tool) that skips category validation would silently turn this into cross-tenant financial data disclosure.
findings.evidence: reports.py:128-141: 'select(sa_func.sum(BudgetAllocation.budgeted_amount)).where(BudgetAllocation.category_id == BudgetCategory.id, BudgetAllocation.month == month_start,).scalar_subquery()' and 'select(sa_func.sum(BudgetTransaction.amount)).where(BudgetTransaction.category_id == BudgetCategory.id, ...date bounds..., BudgetTransaction.deleted_at.is_(None),).scalar_subquery()' — grep of family_id in the file shows the only predicate in this query is the outer 'BudgetCategory.family_id == family_id' (line 148).
findings.recommendation: Add 'BudgetAllocation.family_id == family_id' and 'BudgetTransaction.family_id == family_id' to the two scalar subqueries (both tables have the column). Also worth noting this whole report query is built inline in the route — move it into report_service.py alongside its siblings while touching it.

findings.title: PointTransaction model has no family_id column; points ledger queries scope by user_id only
findings.description: The core points ledger (point_transactions) violates the stated schema rule 'Every model with family data must have family_id as a non-nullable FK to families.id' — the model has only user_id (plus assignment/reward/gig_claim FKs). Consequently every PointsService aggregate (get_total_earned points_service.py:289-296, get_total_spent :299-308, reward redemption count reward_service.py:456-467) filters solely by user_id. Today this is mitigated because callers resolve the target user through get_family_user / current_user before passing the id, but tenancy for the entire points economy rests on that calling convention rather than on the data model — one MCP adapter or admin-adjacent query that accepts a raw user_id crosses families with no second line of defense. This is a legacy-era model (old-style Column declarations, unlike newer Mapped models that all carry family_id) and is not covered by any prior-audit known-open item.
findings.evidence: point_transaction.py:32-53 — full column list is id, type, points, description, user_id, balance_before, balance_after, assignment_id, reward_id, gig_claim_id, created_at, created_by; no family_id. points_service.py:289-292 'query = select(func.sum(PointTransaction.points)).where(and_(PointTransaction.user_id == user_id, PointTransaction.points > 0,))' — no family predicate.
findings.recommendation: Alembic migration: add family_id (FK families.id) backfilled from users.family_id, make it non-nullable, index it; then thread family_id through PointsService signatures and add it to the WHERE clauses so the ledger enforces tenancy at the data layer like every other domain.

findings.title: Jarvis /chat maps every ValidationError to HTTP 502, including user-input errors
findings.description: JarvisService.chat raises ValidationError for at least three distinct conditions: empty message (user error → should be 400/422), daily message cap reached (quota → should be 429), and 'Jarvis chat failed: {exc}' when the upstream LLM call throws (genuine 502, jarvis_service.py:641-642). The route collapses all of them: 'except ValidationError as exc: raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=str(exc))'. A kid hitting the daily cap or submitting an empty message receives 502 Bad Gateway — the client renders it as a service outage, and any 5xx-based alerting/uptime monitoring counts routine quota hits as backend failures. This also bypasses the app-wide domain-exception → status-code translation in exception_handlers.py, which would have produced the right 4xx if the route simply let ValidationError propagate.
findings.evidence: jarvis.py:79-80 'except ValidationError as exc: raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=str(exc))'; jarvis_service.py:578-587 raises ValidationError("Message is empty.") and ValidationError(f"Daily Jarvis cap reached ({cap}). Try again tomorrow.") through the same path as :641 'raise ValidationError(f"Jarvis chat failed: {exc}")'.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a distinct domain exception for upstream-LLM failure (e.g. UpstreamAIError → 502) and let plain ValidationError flow to the registered exception handlers (400); return 429 for the cap. Small change confined to jarvis_service.py + jarvis.py.

findings.title: Scheduler leader election fails open with --workers 2: Redis blip yields two concurrent leaders
findings.description: try_acquire_scheduler_leadership returns leader=True on ANY Redis exception ('fail-open: if Redis is unreachable we return leader=True so a single-instance deploy with no Redis still runs its jobs'). Production runs uvicorn --workers 2 (docker-compose.onprem.yml:95), so if Redis is momentarily unreachable while both workers boot (realistic during deploy-onprem's scoped down/up, when redis may still be starting), BOTH workers become leader and every cron job fires twice concurrently — including _family_bank_payday_sweep and _recurring_post_sweep, which move family money. The payday idempotency guard is a read-then-write check (bank_service compares last_chore_paycheck_week / existing CashTransaction week_of before inserting), which two simultaneous leaders firing at the same cron second can race, double-paying allowances. Secondary gap: renew_scheduler_leadership swallows all failures (lines 88-90 'except Exception: pass') and its Lua return value is never checked, so a leader that loses its lock during a >120s Redis outage keeps its scheduler running while a restarting worker can acquire leadership — same two-leader outcome by a different path.
findings.evidence: scheduler_lock.py:69-74 'except Exception: ... return True, None, None  # fail-open on Redis error' (and :59-60, same at connect); :87-90 'try: await client.eval(_RENEW_LUA, 1, key, token, ttl) except Exception: pass' — return value discarded; docker-compose.onprem.yml:95 'command: uvicorn app.main:app ... --workers 2 --proxy-headers'.
findings.recommendation: Since prod always has Redis, make fail-open configurable and default it OFF when workers > 1 (e.g. retry acquire with backoff for ~30s before deciding, or gate on a SCHEDULER_FAIL_OPEN env). Check the renew Lua result and, on 0 (lock lost), shut the local scheduler down. Cheap insurance for the two money sweeps; add a DB-level unique constraint on (kid, week_of, ALLOWANCE) as belt-and-braces if not present.

findings.title: Allocation auto-fill strategies run one aggregate query per category (N+1)
findings.description: The auto-fill strategy implementations loop over categories issuing a separate SUM query per category: _fill_from_history ('for cat in cats: ... total = (await db.execute(activity_q)).scalar() or 0', lines 1021-1035), _average_n_months (same shape, per-category activity query around line 845), and auto_fill does a per-allocation existence check via _get_allocation_for_category_month in a loop (lines 780-800). Contrast get_categories_available_amounts (line 409), which was explicitly rewritten to replace exactly this per-category N+1 with four grouped queries — the batched pattern already exists in the same file. Bounded impact (parent-triggered action, typically 20-60 categories → 20-60 extra round-trips), so low severity, but it is the same anti-pattern the file's own docstring calls out as fixed.
findings.evidence: allocation_service.py:1032-1035 'for cat in cats: activity_q = (select(func.coalesce(func.sum(BudgetTransaction.amount), 0))... total = (await db.execute(activity_q)).scalar() or 0' vs :417-419 docstring of the batched sibling: 'Replaces the per-category N+1 (each category ran ~5 queries) with four grouped aggregate queries'.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the three strategy loops to a single GROUP BY category_id aggregate over the date window (identical to _grouped() in get_categories_available_amounts) plus one query fetching existing target-month allocations keyed by category_id.

findings.title: Secondary route-embedded business logic: users.py member rejection, months.py/month.py inline SQL
findings.description: Runner-up layering violations behind subscriptions.py (all smaller but same rule): (1) reject_pending_member (users.py:352-405) embeds the approval-status precondition, a bulk DELETE of the rejected user's open TaskAssignments, and the audit-logging policy directly in the route before delegating the final delete to AuthService — the compensating-delete semantics documented in its long docstring belong in auth_service next to approve_user. (2) months.py month-status route builds the BudgetMonthHold aggregate inline with mid-function imports ('from sqlalchemy import func as sa_func, select' inside the handler, lines 101-110) instead of asking MonthLockingService. (3) month.py get_month_budget (lines 38-157) constructs the income query and performs all group/category totals aggregation in the route (which is where the double-count bug of the separate finding was able to hide). None are security issues; together they are the remaining bulk of untestable-in-isolation logic in the routes tier now that register_family and kiosk are fixed.
findings.evidence: users.py:381-390 'result = await db.execute(sql_delete(TaskAssignment).where(and_(TaskAssignment.assigned_to == user.id, TaskAssignment.status.in_([AssignmentStatus.PENDING, AssignmentStatus.OVERDUE]),)))' inside the route handler; months.py:102-110 inline 'from sqlalchemy import func as sa_func, select ... select(sa_func.coalesce(sa_func.sum(BudgetMonthHold.amount_cents), 0))' in the handler body.
findings.recommendation: Move the rejection flow into AuthService.reject_pending_user (precondition + assignment cleanup + delete in one transaction), the hold aggregate into MonthLockingService.get_month_status, and the month-view assembly into AllocationService (get_month_summary already exists as a stub home). Each is a mechanical extraction with existing tests to lean on.

findings.title: 20 copy-pasted catch-all API proxies (1,635 LOC) with confirmed behavioral drift
findings.description: Every domain has its own hand-copied wildcard proxy under frontend/src/pages/api/*/[...path].ts — 20 files, 1,635 LOC, all reimplementing the same auth-cookie-to-Bearer injection, header forwarding, 401 transparent-refresh, and 502 fallback. They have drifted into two generations: 12 files follow 3xx redirects manually (the fix for the known 'trailing-slash → FastAPI 307 → broken POST body' bug, documented in the admin proxy's own comment), while 8 files (analytics, chat, dm, jarvis, kiosk, meals, referrals, subscriptions) do NOT — they pass the 307 through with an internal http://backend:8000 Location the browser cannot reach. 4 files (analytics, chat, jarvis, referrals) also lack the PATCH export the others have. Every copy carries the same dead `const path = params.path ?? ""` line. This is the highest LOC-saved x correctness-risk item in the repo: a security-sensitive (token-handling) block whose past bugfixes provably failed to propagate to all copies.
findings.evidence: gigs/[...path].ts:56 has `if (backendRes.status >= 300 && backendRes.status < 400) { ... return doFetch(redirectUrl); }` while chat/[...path].ts (57 lines) has no such block and ends at `export const DELETE` with no PATCH. Verified via `grep -c 'export const PATCH' / 'status >= 300'` across all 20: PATCH=0 for analytics/chat/jarvis/referrals; redirect-follow=0 for analytics/chat/dm/jarvis/kiosk/meals/referrals/subscriptions. admin/[...path].ts comment: 'It uses url.pathname rather than params.path because rebuilding the path drops the trailing slash and FastAPI's 307 then breaks the proxied POST body.'
findings.recommendation: Extract a `createApiProxy(opts)` factory into frontend/src/lib/server/proxy.ts (options: label for error logs, skipAuthPaths for kiosk's token-gated /snapshot, methods list). Each route file collapses to ~5 lines (`export const { GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH } = createApiProxy({...})`). Bring all 20 to the newest behavior (redirect-follow + PATCH + refresh-cookie propagation). Saves ~1,400 LOC and makes the next proxy bugfix a one-file change. Risk: low-medium — behavior is fully understood, kiosk is the only genuine variant; smoke-test chat/dm SSE-adjacent paths after unifying.

findings.title: Duplicated grade-credit math: parent payouts dashboard can show 1 point less than the kid was actually awarded
findings.description: Partial-grade credit scaling is computed in four places with three different rounding conventions. task_assignment_service.py awards points half-up: `(effective_points * award_pct + 50) // 100` (lines 1718 and 2040 — its own comment says '25 pts x 50% -> 13, not 12'). bank_service._chore_week_tasks line 482 computes the parent payouts dashboard's `earned` for the SAME assignments with Python's `round(pts * credit_pct / 100)` — banker's rounding, so 12.5 rounds DOWN to 12. For any assignment where points x pct ends in exactly .5 (e.g. 25 pts graded partial at 50%), the kid is awarded 13 points but the parent payouts dashboard shows 12. The duplicated `credit_pct = int(pct or 50) if grade == "partial" else 100` line also appears twice in bank_service (431 and 480), and _chore_week_tasks's docstring (line 444) admits the bucket rules 'must stay in lockstep with _chore_units' — lockstep enforced only by hope.
findings.evidence: bank_service.py:482 `bucket, earned = "credited", round(pts * credit_pct / 100)` vs task_assignment_service.py:2040 `pts = (assignment.template.effective_points * award_pct + 50) // 100` (comment at 2038: 'Integer half-up so partial credit never silently floors away a point (25 pts × 50% → 13, not 12)'). Python `round(12.5)` == 12 (half-even), `(1250 + 50) // 100` == 13.
findings.recommendation: Extract one shared helper (e.g. app/core/grading.py or points_service): `grade_credit_points(points, pct) -> int` using the canonical half-up formula, plus a `grade_credit_units(points, pct)` for the x100 paycheck-unit variant. Replace all four sites (task_assignment_service.py:1718,2040; bank_service.py:431-434,480-482). Fixes the display/award mismatch and makes the lockstep contract structural. Add a test asserting dashboard earned == awarded points for a 25-pt/50% partial.

findings.title: Client mutation handling fragmented across 4 competing conventions despite purpose-built shared helpers
findings.description: lib/mutate.ts and lib/toast.ts were built (UX audit waves) specifically to replace the fetch->alert->location.reload() pattern, but adoption stalled: only 4 pages use mutate() and 12 use the shared showToast, while 45 raw `alert()` call sites remain across 15 pages, 77 `location.reload()` sites remain (budget/settings.astro alone has 27, budget/transactions.astro 11), and 6 pages define their own private showToast (routines.astro:193, pet.astro:275, pet/quests.astro:247, pet/shop.astro:180, parent/routines.astro:224, budget/settings.astro:581 — the last a fully divergent implementation with its own DOM element and styling). Each reload re-runs a full SSR page (4-8 serial API calls) for one change; each alert() is a UX regression vs the toast system on the pages that do use it. Net: the same ~10-line try/fetch/res.ok/error-surface/reload block is hand-rolled at roughly 60-80 sites (87 client `fetch('/api` sites, 64 `.ok` checks, 125 catch blocks).
findings.evidence: budget/settings.astro:581 `function showToast(msg, type = "success") { const t = document.getElementById("settings-toast"); ... }` coexisting with lib/toast.ts's exported showToast; grep counts: `alert(` = 45 sites/15 pages, `location.reload()` = 77 sites, `lib/mutate` imported by 4 pages, shared showToast used by 12 of 91 pages.
findings.recommendation: Incremental migration, worst pages first (budget/settings, budget/transactions, parent/gigs, gigs/my-gigs): replace alert() with showToast and reload-after-write with mutate() where a reload isn't structurally required. For the 6 local-showToast pages the blocker is `define:vars` inline scripts (cannot import modules) — either expose the shared toast on `window` from ToastContainer.astro or convert those scripts to module scripts with data-attributes. Estimated ~300-500 LOC removed plus the perf win of killing serial-SSR reloads. Risk: low per page but wide surface — do it page-by-page behind the existing e2e suite.

findings.title: LLM client scaffolding copy-pasted across 7 call sites; AI services depend on the budget receipt scanner for core LLM constants
findings.description: Seven sites in six services construct the identical OpenAI-over-LiteLLM client — `OpenAI(base_url=f"{settings.LITELLM_API_BASE.rstrip('/')}/v1", api_key=settings.LITELLM_API_KEY, timeout=LLM_TIMEOUT)` plus the same 'not configured. Set LITELLM_API_KEY' guard and the same '# connect fails fast; read capped at 60s' comment: jarvis_service.py:413,615; calendar_scanner_service.py:98; recipe_importer.py:97; task_proof_validator.py:108; budget/category_ai_service.py:115; budget/receipt_scanner_service.py:273. Worse than the LOC: jarvis, calendar, recipe and proof-validator all import LLM_TIMEOUT (and RECEIPT_MODEL) from app/services/budget/receipt_scanner_service.py, making a budget-domain service the de-facto LLM core module (wrong dependency direction — CLAUDE.md even documents receipt_scanner as 'also exports the shared LLM_TIMEOUT'). translation_service.py has silently diverged: raw httpx POST to /v1/chat/completions with its own hardcoded `timeout=30.0` and no connect-fail-fast, so translation is the one LLM path not covered by the shared timeout policy.
findings.evidence: jarvis_service.py:39 `from app.services.budget.receipt_scanner_service import LLM_TIMEOUT, RECEIPT_MODEL`; same import in recipe_importer.py:21, task_proof_validator.py:23, calendar_scanner_service.py:26; translation_service.py:70 `async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30.0) as client:` vs receipt_scanner_service.py:59 `LLM_TIMEOUT = httpx.Timeout(LLM_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, connect=5.0)`.
findings.recommendation: Create app/core/llm.py owning LLM_TIMEOUT, model aliases (RECEIPT_MODEL etc.), a `get_llm_client()` factory that raises the domain 'not configured' ValidationError, and optionally a thin chat-completion wrapper translation_service can use. Repoint the six services' imports; receipt_scanner keeps re-exporting for back-compat one release. ~80-120 LOC saved; the real wins are correct dependency direction, one place to change timeout/retry policy, and a single chokepoint to audit the 'every LLM call site premium-gated' rule against.

findings.title: Hand-rolled modal overlay shell duplicated ~10x across pages plus 30 native confirm() dialogs
findings.description: The exact overlay shell string `hidden fixed inset-0 z-[60] flex items-end sm:items-center justify-center bg-black/50 backdrop-blur-sm px-4` is copy-pasted across pages (bank.astro:299,325; gigs/index.astro:247; parent/settings/family-bank.astro:452,490; parent/tasks.astro:380 near-variant; 35 `fixed inset-0` sites total across 12 pages + components), alongside 8+ bespoke one-off *Modal.astro components (TaskCreateModal, AccountCreateModal, AssignFundsModal, MoveMoneyModal, EditMemberModal, InvitationModal, FABModal, CoverOverspendingModal) that each re-implement open/close/backdrop logic. Separately, 30 native `confirm()` call sites do destructive-action confirmation with the browser dialog instead of any styled component. The project's own hard rule — modals must be z-[60] with z-[55] backdrop to clear BottomNav — is currently enforced only by convention in each copy; the orphaned ui/BottomSheet.astro (known-open finding, not re-reported) appears to be the abandoned attempt at exactly this extraction.
findings.evidence: Identical class string at bank.astro:299 `<div id="bank-modal" class="hidden fixed inset-0 z-[60] flex items-end sm:items-center justify-center bg-black/50 backdrop-blur-sm px-4">`, gigs/index.astro:247, parent/settings/family-bank.astro:452. grep counts: `fixed inset-0` = 35 sites; bare `confirm(` = 30 sites.
findings.recommendation: Extract a slotted `Modal.astro` (shell + backdrop + open/close + z-[60]/z-[55] baked in, safe-area padding) and a `ConfirmDialog` helper; either revive BottomSheet.astro for the mobile sheet variant or delete it. Migrate the raw page-level modals first (bank, gigs, family-bank, parent/tasks), then rebase the bespoke *Modal components on the shell. ~200-400 LOC saved; correctness win is centralizing the z-index/safe-area rule that has already caused mobile bugs per project memory. Risk: medium — each modal's close/submit wiring is bespoke vanilla JS; migrate incrementally with the Playwright suite.

findings.title: Inline kid-role gates still repeated across bank/gigs/rewards routes (open since 07-22 audit)
findings.description: Still open from the 2026-07-22 audit: bank.py defines a local `_require_kid` helper (line 67) but uses it at only 2 of its 9 kid-gate sites — the other 7 (78, 126, 154, 202, 297, 381, 405) inline `if current_user.role == UserRole.PARENT: raise HTTPException(...)`; gigs.py:216 and rewards.py:87,108 repeat the same inline pattern (rewards.py:108 at least uses the domain ForbiddenException). No shared `require_kid_role` dependency exists in core/dependencies.py even though `require_parent_role` does. Nuance a naive extraction must respect: the variants intentionally differ — bank.py:78 and 126 return 400 with a pointer to the parent endpoint, rewards.py:71 returns None for parents, and the raise sites split between HTTPException-403 and ForbiddenException.
findings.evidence: bank.py:67 `def _require_kid(user: User) -> None: if user.role not in (UserRole.CHILD, UserRole.TEEN): raise HTTPException(status_code=403, ...)` used only at lines 342,356, while bank.py:78 in the same file inlines `if current_user.role == UserRole.PARENT: raise HTTPException(status_code=400, ...)`; gigs.py:216-220 inlines a 403.
findings.recommendation: Add `require_kid_role` (CHILD/TEEN) to app/core/dependencies.py raising the domain ForbiddenException, adopt it at the plain-403 sites (bank x5-7, gigs x2, rewards x1), and leave the deliberate 400-with-pointer and return-None sites as-is with a comment. ~30-40 LOC saved; the value is making the kid-gate greppable/auditable rather than 4 spellings of it.

findings.title: Amount-tolerance math still duplicated between dedup_service and duplicate_guard_service (open since 07-22 audit)
findings.description: Unchanged since flagged 2026-07-22: both duplicate-detection services independently define `AMOUNT_TOLERANCE = 0.01` and the identical `tol = max(1, int(abs(...) * cls.AMOUNT_TOLERANCE))` clamp (dedup_service.py:57,108; duplicate_guard_service.py:31,44). Only 2 copies and both currently agree, so the risk is drift-if-tuned: if the +/-1% window is ever adjusted for one flow (scan-time guard vs batch dedup), the other silently diverges and 'is this a duplicate transaction' means two different things in the same module.
findings.evidence: dedup_service.py:108 `tol = max(1, int(abs(int(a.amount)) * cls.AMOUNT_TOLERANCE))` vs duplicate_guard_service.py:44 `tol = max(1, int(abs(amount_cents) * cls.AMOUNT_TOLERANCE))`, each with its own `AMOUNT_TOLERANCE = 0.01` class constant.
findings.recommendation: Extract `amount_tolerance_cents(amount_cents, pct=0.01) -> int` into a tiny shared module (e.g. budget/_matching.py) and use it from both services (and any future account_matching/a2a matcher). ~6 LOC saved; the point is a single tunable definition of 'same amount'.

findings.title: Family-scoped get-or-404 boilerplate hand-rolled in services that skip BaseFamilyService
findings.description: BaseFamilyService.get_by_id already provides the select-by-id+family_id+NotFoundException pattern (including soft-delete awareness), and 18 services extend it — but shopping_service, meal_service, calendar_service and family_chat_service hand-roll the same ~6-line lookup repeatedly (shopping_service.py:85-101 get_list, 164-167 item lookup; meal_service.py:88-93 get_recipe, 250-255 and 272-277 meal-entry lookups; 57 `raise NotFoundException` sites across services overall). Each copy is tenant-isolation-critical code (the family_id filter IS the multi-tenant boundary), so every hand-rolled instance is one more place a future edit can drop the filter.
findings.evidence: shopping_service.py:98-101 `lst = (await db.execute(q)).scalar_one_or_none()\n if not lst:\n raise NotFoundException("Shopping list not found")` — structurally identical to meal_service.py:90-93 and to BaseFamilyService.get_by_id (base_service.py:64-76).
findings.recommendation: Not a mass migration: where the lookup needs eager-loads, keep local queries. But the plain lookups (meal entries, shopping items) can extend BaseFamilyService or call a module-level `get_scoped_or_404(db, Model, id, family_id, options=...)` helper added to base_service.py. ~60-100 LOC saved; main value is shrinking the surface where a family_id filter could be forgotten.

findings.title: Recycle-bin service: 07-22 P1 duplication largely FIXED; only the two cascade-restore bodies remain near-identical
findings.description: Status update so this is not re-reported as new: the 2026-07-22 P1 (4x near-duplicate restore/delete families, Python-side cutoff filtering, unused SUPPORTED_MODELS) is now fixed — shared `_restore`/`_permanently_delete` helpers exist (lines 143-195), restore_category/restore_category_group delegate, `empty_recycle_bin` pushes the cutoff into SQL (`model.deleted_at < cutoff`, line 388) and iterates SUPPORTED_MODELS. Residual duplication: `restore_transaction` (198-232) and `restore_account` (234-272) are ~30-line near-twins — same select/guard, same `cascade_ts = x.deleted_at` capture, same bulk `sql_update(BudgetTransaction)...values(deleted_at=None, deleted_by_id=None)`, same commit+refresh — differing only in the cascade WHERE column (parent_id vs account_id). Also `list_deleted_items` (40-141) repeats the same 12-line select block 4x, one per model, though SUPPORTED_MODELS could drive it.
findings.evidence: restore_transaction:220-228 and restore_account:259-267 both end in `.values(deleted_at=None, deleted_by_id=None)` after capturing `cascade_ts`; the only structural difference is `BudgetTransaction.parent_id == transaction_id` vs `BudgetTransaction.account_id == account_id`.
findings.recommendation: Optional polish, not urgent: fold both into `_restore_with_cascade(db, model, item_id, family_id, cascade_column)` and drive list_deleted_items off SUPPORTED_MODELS (~50 LOC saved). Main deliverable of this finding is the status correction: do not re-open the 07-22 P1 as-written.

findings.title: Receipt-image persistence is GCS-only and silently dead on the canonical on-prem prod
findings.description: The entire receipt-image subsystem is hard-wired to Google Cloud Storage from the decommissioned GCP era, with no local/on-prem backend. On successful scans, `GCSReceiptStorage.upload()` is called unconditionally inside a swallow-all try/except (receipt_scanner_service.py:866-888, 'GCS upload skipped for txn %s'); the serving endpoint `GET /api/budget/transactions/{id}/receipt` (backend/app/api/routes/budget/transactions.py:246) reads only from GCS. `GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET` defaults to "" (config.py:221), is absent from .env.onprem.example, and on-prem 10.1.0.91 has no GCE metadata server for ADC — so `storage.Client()` fails, the exception is swallowed, `receipt_image_path` stays NULL, and every scanned receipt's original image has been silently discarded since the 2026-07-05 cutover (the receipt endpoint then 404s 'no receipt image'). The codebase already acknowledges this state: family_deletion_service.py:231 'If GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET is unset (e.g. on-prem), the keys point at nothing reachable from this environment; skip without failing.' Only receipt DRAFTS go to local disk (UPLOADS_ROOT/receipt-drafts); approved-scan originals do not. The requirements.txt:87 comment ('VM service account has roles/storage.objectAdmin... ADC via metadata server') is also stale GCP doc.
findings.evidence: receipt_scanner_service.py:866-888: `from app.services.storage.gcs_receipt_service import GCSReceiptStorage / gcs_path = GCSReceiptStorage.upload(...)` ... `except Exception: ... logger.exception("GCS upload skipped for txn %s", txn.id)`; family_deletion_service.py:231: "If GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET is unset (e.g. on-prem), the keys point at nothing reachable from this environment; skip without failing."; grep GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET .env.onprem.example → no hits; config.py:221 `GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET: str = ""`
findings.recommendation: First confirm prod .env on 10.1.0.91 really lacks GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET (no template or doc provides it, so almost certainly yes). Then add a local-volume storage backend behind the same upload/download/delete interface (pattern already exists: gig proofs and receipt drafts under settings.UPLOADS_ROOT, backed up by family-onprem-backup), select backend on GCS_RECEIPT_BUCKET presence, and make the scan path stop swallowing a permanently-failing upload. Alternatively drop the GCS path + google-cloud-storage dependency entirely if the bucket is not coming back.

findings.title: authlib==1.3.0 is pinned in prod requirements but has zero imports anywhere — and the pinned version carries CVE-2024-37568
findings.description: `authlib==1.3.0` ships in the production image but is imported nowhere: `grep -rn authlib backend --include='*.py'` (app, tests, scripts, seeds, conftest; .venv excluded) returns zero hits. Auth is PyJWT (own tokens) + google-auth (OAuth ID-token verification); nothing pulls authlib transitively. The pinned 1.3.0 predates the CVE-2024-37568 fix (JWS algorithm-confusion, fixed in 1.3.1; latest is 1.7.2). Not exploitable while unimported, but it is a vulnerable library sitting in the prod image for no reason. The 2026-07-22 audit flagged authlib as 'stale, worth priority review' — the simpler truth is it is entirely unused.
findings.evidence: requirements.txt:30 `authlib==1.3.0`; `grep -rn "authlib" backend --include="*.py" | grep -v .venv` → no output; PyPI latest 1.7.2
findings.recommendation: Delete the pin from requirements.txt, rebuild, run the full suite (expect green — nothing imports it). Closes a scanner-bait CVE surface and shrinks the image for free.

findings.title: mcp==1.12.4 is the keystone pin freezing the whole web stack (starlette<0.42 → fastapi 0.115.6)
findings.description: requirements.txt:4 documents the chain explicitly: 'starlette is pinned to <0.42.0 because mcp==1.12.4 pulls sse-starlette 3.4.5 which would otherwise upgrade starlette to 1.x — incompatible with fastapi 0.115.6'. mcp is now at 1.28.1 (16 minors behind), fastapi at 0.140.1 vs pinned 0.115.6, redis-py at 8.0.1 vs pinned 5.0.1, plus alembic 1.13.1 / sqlalchemy 2.0.25 / asyncpg 0.29.0 / uvicorn 0.27.0 all ~18 months old. General staleness was flagged 2026-07-22; the new actionable insight is the causal order: bumping mcp first dissolves the sse-starlette/starlette ceiling, which then unlocks fastapi/starlette (both security-relevant — starlette/fastapi have had recurring multipart/DoS fixes, as this file's own line 2 CVE note shows this app cares about).
findings.evidence: requirements.txt:4 '# starlette is pinned to <0.42.0 because mcp==1.12.4 pulls sse-starlette 3.4.5'; :6 `fastapi==0.115.6`; :96 `mcp==1.12.4`; PyPI: mcp 1.28.1, fastapi 0.140.1, redis 8.0.1
findings.recommendation: One dedicated bump PR in dependency order: mcp → sse-starlette/starlette → fastapi → (separately) redis 5→8 which has breaking API changes. Full pytest + the Jarvis MCP suite are the safety net; the migrations round-trip in CI covers alembic. Do it before the gap forces a big-bang upgrade under CVE pressure.

findings.title: Floor-only pins (openai>=, pymupdf>=, google-cloud-storage>=) make prod image builds non-reproducible
findings.description: Everything in requirements.txt is ==pinned except `openai>=1.50.0` (line 53), `pymupdf>=1.24.0` (line 58) and `google-cloud-storage>=2.18` (line 87). deploy-onprem.sh builds a fresh image at every deploy, so whatever PyPI serves that day lands in prod untested — an openai 2.x major (SDK with heavy churn history) or a pymupdf ABI change would break receipt scanning at deploy time, not in CI (CI installs the same floating floors, but at a different date than the prod build). This is the exact failure mode already memorialized in this project ('dev container masks requirements conflicts that only break clean prod builds').
findings.evidence: requirements.txt:53 `openai>=1.50.0`, :58 `pymupdf>=1.24.0`, :87 `google-cloud-storage>=2.18` — the only non-== entries besides the intentional starlette range
findings.recommendation: Pin all three to the currently-installed exact versions (get them from the running prod container: `podman exec family_onprem_backend pip show openai pymupdf google-cloud-storage`), keeping the explanatory comments. If the GCS finding above ends in removal, google-cloud-storage goes away instead.

findings.title: Env-template drift: dead vars operators are told to set, and live vars (VAPID, LiteLLM) missing from templates
findings.description: Both directions of .env-example ↔ config.py parity are broken. Dead vars in templates: `.env.onprem.example:24 JWT_SECRET_KEY=CHANGE_ME_...` — nothing reads JWT_SECRET_KEY (config.py uses SECRET_KEY; only other mention is a docker-compose.yml:80 comment), so operators generate and rotate a secret that does nothing; `.env.onprem.example:44 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` and `config.py:215 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: str = ""` have zero readers in app code (all LLM traffic goes through LITELLM_API_BASE/KEY per CLAUDE.md); `.env.example:35-36 SMTP_FROM_EMAIL/SMTP_FROM_NAME` are not settings fields (config reads EMAIL_FROM/EMAIL_FROM_NAME). Missing vars: VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY/VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY/VAPID_CLAIM_EMAIL appear in NEITHER template even though scripts/generate-vapid-keys.py exists and push_service.py:7 documents that unset keys silently disable web push ('sends are skipped with a warning') — a fresh operator bootstrap ships prod with parent gig-approval push notifications off and no signal. `.env.example` (which CLAUDE.md's env table points to) also lacks LITELLM_API_BASE/KEY, PAYPAL_*, RESEND_API_KEY, SENTRY_DSN entirely.
findings.evidence: .env.onprem.example:24 `JWT_SECRET_KEY=CHANGE_ME_openssl_rand_hex_32` + `grep -rn JWT_SECRET_KEY backend/app` → 0 hits; config.py:215 `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: str = ""` sole occurrence in backend/app; push_service.py:7 'If VAPID keys are not configured, sends are skipped with a warning'; comm-diff of config.py fields vs both templates (VAPID_* absent from both)
findings.recommendation: One small PR: delete JWT_SECRET_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from .env.onprem.example + docker-compose comment, delete the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY settings field, fix SMTP_FROM_* → EMAIL_FROM/EMAIL_FROM_NAME in .env.example, and add VAPID_* (with a pointer to scripts/generate-vapid-keys.py) plus LITELLM_* / PAYPAL_* / RESEND_API_KEY stubs to the templates. Then verify prod .env on .91 actually has VAPID keys set.

findings.title: Ruff gate misses blocking-I/O-in-async: 12 verified ASYNC violations in request paths
findings.description: ruff.toml runs only the default E4/E7/E9/F set plus DTZ ('widen gradually' is stated intent, but nothing has widened since). Running `ruff check app --select B,ASYNC` today: 6× ASYNC230 (blocking `open()` inside async defs: api/routes/task_assignments.py:225,234; services/budget/receipt_scanner_service.py:1175,1181; services/email_service.py:1165; services/task_proof_validator.py:59), 5× ASYNC240, 1× ASYNC109, 60× B904 (raise-without-from in except), 856× B008 (pure FastAPI `Depends(...)` idiom noise — must be ignored if B is enabled). The ASYNC230 sites are sync disk writes/reads of user-uploaded proof photos and receipts on the single event loop — multi-MB uploads stall every concurrent request, the same class of bug this repo already codified for DB sessions (SSE no-pooled-session rule).
findings.evidence: `ruff check app --select B,ASYNC` → 'Found 931 errors'; breakdown: 856 B008, 60 B904, 6 ASYNC230, 5 ASYNC240, 2 B007, 1 B905, 1 ASYNC109; e.g. task_assignments.py:225 'ASYNC230 Async functions should not open files with blocking methods like `open`'
findings.recommendation: Add `"ASYNC"` to extend-select now and fix the 12 sites (wrap in `asyncio.to_thread`, matching the pywebpush pattern already used in push_service). Enable `"B"` with `ignore B008` as a follow-up (B904 fixes are mechanical `raise ... from e`).

findings.title: Two phantom no-op migrations with misleading names sit in the alembic chain
findings.description: Chain health is otherwise good: single head (`user_last_seen_at`), 114 revision files. But `fab16872eb7e_add_email_verification_tokens_table` and `8d23a3796561_add_password_reset_tokens_table` (both 2025-12-12) have `pass` for BOTH upgrade() and downgrade() — the tables their filenames promise are actually created three months later inside `a6d655cbc18c_add_assignment_type_to_task_templates.py:21,35` (itself a misnamed autogenerate rollup). Anyone doing schema archaeology on the token tables greps to the wrong revisions. Note also that CI's round-trip only exercises `downgrade -1` from head, so deeper irreversible downgrades (e.g. 2026_05_25_drop_stripe.py's `pass`) are never validated — acceptable, but worth knowing the round-trip claim covers one step only.
findings.evidence: fab16872eb7e lines 19-27: `def upgrade() -> None: ... pass` / `def downgrade() -> None: ... pass` (identical in 8d23a3796561); `grep -n email_verification_tokens backend/migrations/versions/*.py` → created in 2026_03_02_0430-a6d655cbc18c:21
findings.recommendation: Do not delete mid-chain files (breaks deployed alembic_version histories). Add a one-line docstring to each phantom ('no-op; table actually created in a6d655cbc18c') — or fold them away whenever the chain is next squashed to a new baseline.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md count drift: 107→114 migrations, ~1760→1982 tests, '17 budget tables' vs 16
findings.description: Three verified stale counts in CLAUDE.md: line 293 claims 'Single-head chain (107 revisions as of 2026-07-22)' — actual is 114 files today and 111 already existed on 07-22, so the number was wrong when written (the same off-by-N happened in the 07-22 audit, which corrected 102→106); line 286 claims '~1760 tests' — `pytest --collect-only` collects 1982; line 253 (Key files table) says 'All 17 budget tables' while line 158 correctly says '16 budget models' — actual `__tablename__` count in models/budget.py is 16. Counts that drift every few weeks train readers to distrust the doc.
findings.evidence: `ls backend/migrations/versions/*.py | wc -l` → 114; `pytest --collect-only -q` → '1982 tests collected'; `grep -c __tablename__`-equivalent regex on models/budget.py → 16 tables; CLAUDE.md:158 '16 budget models' vs :253 'All 17 budget tables' vs :293 '107 revisions'
findings.recommendation: Fix the three numbers (or better, soften to unqualified phrasing: 'single-head chain; CI exercises the round-trip', '~2000 tests') so they stop rotting. Fold into the next routine CLAUDE.md touch — not worth a dedicated PR.

findings.title: TODO/FIXME sweep and cruft checks: no new debt markers; previously-flagged worktree cruft confirmed cleaned
findings.description: Full repo sweep (backend/app, frontend/src, scripts, e2e-tests) found 12 marker hits, zero new: 2 real TODOs, both already tracked in the 2026-07-22 audit (budget/month.py:177 'Add income tracking'; budget/transfer_service.py:335 actual-spend calc for cover-overspending); 3 known legal placeholders (privacidad.astro:54,165,274 — tracked operator gap); 7 false positives (I-XXXX/P-XXXX/XXXX format examples in subscriptions.py:314, paypal_service.py:141,147, file_import_service.py:128, receipt_scanner_service.py:205; Spanish 'TODAS/TODOS' in parent/settings/family.astro:99). Verified-clean on the rest of the dimension: the 7.2MB orphaned `.claude/worktrees/agent-a34bc264adae2ec80` worktree from the 07-22 audit is gone (`git worktree list` → main only; `.claude/worktrees/` and `.worktrees/` are now empty ignored dirs); docker-compose.stage.yml is a real base-file override since 07-08, not stale fiction; scripts/ has no new cruft (family-backup.* clearly headed 'LEGACY — GCP...
